gap: The British official history could be read only to page 176 (22 October)
effect on the data: British positions after 22 October come from two popular histories of 1916 and from editors' notes in the German account. They are thinner and less exact than the first four days.
how to close it: Read chapters VI to XVIII of the 1925 volume and, above all, its daily situation maps (maps 11 to 39).
v6 update: Partly closed: the bound sketch maps (Sketches 4, 7 to 10, 12 to 14) are now in hand and are in the playback as a backdrop. They have not yet been used to correct the rows.
v7 update: Largely closed for the Allied side: British and French lines for 21, 23, 25, 29 and 31 October and 4, 9 and 11 November are now read from Sketches 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14. The text after page 176 is still unread.

effect on the data: French divisions are placed from British and German accounts. Several rows say only that a French division was somewhere in a sector, and two do not know which division held the line.
how to close it: Read the French official history (Les armees francaises dans la Grande Guerre, tome I, volume 4) and its maps.
v7 update: Partly closed: the sketches give the French sectors, by commander or corps, on the eight dates above. Four inferred French rows are withdrawn and replaced. Still no French source.

gap: German positions rest on one account
effect on the data: The 1917 General Staff monograph is written at corps level and to a purpose. Divisions are placed only where it happens to name them.
how to close it: Read the German official history (Der Weltkrieg, volume 5 and 6) and a modern study such as Sheldon (2010).
v7 update: Unchanged, and now sharper: German lines are text placed against a mapped Allied line (YG15).

gap: Positions were not taken from a period map
effect on the data: Every coordinate is a modern village centre or a point worked out from one. A line "at Zandvoorde" is drawn through the church, not along the trenches.
how to close it: Georeference the official history's situation maps, as was done with Bachelder for Gettysburg.
v6 update: Partly closed: Sketch A of the official history is georeferenced and is a base map in the playback. Ten places have been re-read from it. The unit lines still come from text, not from the dated sketches.
v7 update: Closed for the Allied side on the eight sketch dates; open for the German side and for the days between.

gap: Sector lines are straight lines between named places
effect on the data: The front between two villages is drawn straight. Opposing lines are held apart by offsets I chose, so the width of no man's land on the map means nothing.
how to close it: Trace the lines from period maps. Until then the playback should be read as a diagram.
v7 update: Closed for the rows read from sketches, which follow the drawn line with 2 to 10 points. Still true of the German rows and of the Allied rows that rest on text.

gap: Some hamlets and features are placed from memory
effect on the data: About two dozen places (Koekuit, Kortekeer Cabaret, Klein Zillebeke, Zwarteleen, Hooge, Terhand, Garde Dieu, the canal bend and others) are not in the OpenStreetMap extract and carry coord_source "estimate". They are listed on the Places sheet.
how to close it: Look each up on a 1914 trench map or the Belgian topographic map.
v6 update: Ten of these places (Terhand, Klein Zillebeke, Zwarteleen, Hooge, Garde Dieu, Poezelhoek, the Gheluvelt cross-roads, Herenthage chateau and wood, the woods north-east of Klein Zillebeke) are now read from Sketch A. Terhand had been 880 m out and Poezelhoek 670 m.

gap: Quotations came through a reading tool
effect on the data: The long sources were read in 100,000-character pieces by a tool that returns extracts. The quoted wording is short and probably exact, but none of it has been checked against the page.
how to close it: Check each quotation against the page before anything is published. The Sources sheet marks every one "No" under page verified.

effect on the data: A row ends the day before the next row for the same unit unless a source gives the date. Where the sources stop following a unit the end is "unknown" and the playback shows its last recorded position.
how to close it: Daily situation maps would settle most of these.
v7 update: Unchanged. Rows read from a sketch run to the day before the next sketch; that is a convention, not a source date.

gap: Improvised groups are only partly modelled
effect on the data: Bulfin's and Cavan's forces, Moussy's and Vidal's detachments, Stetten's cavalry group and Group Urach cut across divisions. Two are in the data as units; the rest are mentioned in notes. A division can be in two places at once when part of it is detached.
how to close it: Decide whether a detachment is a unit, an assignment or a note. For now: a unit when the sources place it on its own for more than a day.
v7 update: The sketches name more such groups: de Mitry, Hély d'Oissel, Vidal, Moussy, Woillemont, Olleris, Cavan. Each is now a row or a unit; what each was made of is still not recorded.

gap: Nothing below division, and the edges are cut off
effect on the data: Brigades and regiments are left out. The British II Corps at La Bassee and the 6th Division at Armentieres are south of the map; the German Marine Division and the fighting at Nieuport are barely touched.
how to close it: A second pass at brigade level for the crisis days (29 October to 2 November, 11 November) would test the zoom from operational to tactical scale.
v7 update: The dated sketches end about 9.5 km north and 14.5 km south of Ypres; rows read from them stop at those edges.

effect on the data: The Assignments table has no strength for any Ypres unit.
how to close it: The official histories give ration strengths for some dates.

gap: Outside datasets do not cover the battle
effect on the data: Neither CDB90 nor the War Atlas dataset has a record for First Ypres (both have Second and Third Ypres). Only the war and the battle carry a Wikidata ID.
how to close it: Look up Wikidata IDs for the three sub-battles, Messines 1914 and the Yser, and for the divisions.

effect on the data: Polygon Wood, Nonne Bosschen and Houthulst Forest are drawn from the bounding boxes of their modern outlines. Herenthage wood and the woods round Klein Zillebeke are not drawn at all.
how to close it: Take the 1914 wood outlines from a period map.
v6 update: Unchanged, but Sketch A shows the 1914 woods and can be traced.

gap: Boundaries between formations are not marked on the sketches
effect on the data: Where one division stops and the next begins is put at breaks in the drawn line or at the ends of labels. The French XVI Corps line of 4 to 11 November is one row for several divisions because they cannot be separated.
how to close it: The French official history and its maps; British divisional war diaries.

gap: The sketches show German formations as arrows, not lines
effect on the data: German rows still take their places from the German account. Where that would put them on or behind the Allied line as mapped, the points are moved 500 m clear of it and marked "derived".
how to close it: German divisional histories or the Reichsarchiv maps.

gap: Only the last line on each sketch was read
effect on the data: Each sketch covers two to five days and draws the line of each; only the latest (the solid line) is in the data. Days between sketch dates keep the earlier line or fall back on the text, so the British line of 26 to 28 and 30 October and of 1 to 3 and 5 to 8 November is the least sure.
how to close it: Read the dashed and dotted lines on Sketches 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14.

effect on the data: They are larger-scale views (the situation on 20 October, Gheluvelt on 31 October, the situation on 10 November and the Guard attack of 11 November). The Gheluvelt and Nonne Bosschen rows are less exact than they could be.
how to close it: Georeference and read them the same way.
